title: What You Practice Is as Important as How You Practice
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This essay argues that the focus of practice matters as much as the commitment to practicing at all, since performers left without guidance tend to gravitate toward rehearsing what they're already comfortable with rather than what most needs work. It frames coaches as essential precisely for this reason: directing attention to the highest-leverage skills, whether weaknesses or under-practiced fundamentals, and designing drills specific enough to accelerate real improvement. Several well-known examples -- Steph Curry's covered-basket jump-shot drill, Pistol Pete Maravich's car-dribbling routine, Serena Williams's close-range ball spins, Roger Clemens's string-frame pitching target -- illustrate how elite performers use inventive, purpose-built drills rather than generic repetition.
points: What a performer practices, in what sequence, and with what feedback matters as much as the commitment to practice itself.
Without guidance, performers tend to rehearse skills they're already good at rather than the ones that would most improve their performance.
Coaches add value primarily by directing practice toward the highest-leverage areas, whether weaknesses or under-practiced fundamentals.
Elite performers often use unusual, purpose-built drills: Steph Curry's covered-basket jump shots, Pistol Pete Maravich's car-dribbling, Serena Williams's close-range ball spins.
The best performers' edge often comes from having found drills that develop their skills faster than the generic practices their competitors use.
quotes: A solid practice session helps performers identify what changes to make and what actions to amplify.
What a performer practices, in what sequence, and with what feedback matters as much as the commitment to practice does.
Without guidance or oversight, it is common for performers to practice things that don't make them any better.
Directing performers to those areas where practice is most needed is a game-changer.
Examine the practice sessions of a world-class performer in any arena, and you will likely find unique and difficult practice drills no one else has ever heard of.
What a performer practices matters as much, if not more, than the practice itself.
